clue.text: What the Poet Laureate did when tired (and emotional?)

definitions.text: What the Poet Laureate did when tired (and emotional?)

parts.words: What the Poet Laureate did when tired (and emotional?)
parts.note: the Poet Laureate was traditionally paid partly in sack (sherry), so when weary he went to bed, or when 'tired and emotional' (drunk) he had got stuck into his wine

explanation.surface: A question about the habits of Britain's official court poet at the end of a long day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tired and emotional' is a British euphemism for drunk. The Poet Laureate's traditional fee included a butt of sack, a fortified wine like sherry, so 'sack' is both bed and his drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for going to bed, and here also for attacking the sherry the laureate was paid in.

clue.text: Consent to marry Chinese daughter

parts.note: the Han are the majority ethnic group of China

explanation.surface: A suitor wins agreement to wed a Chinese man's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for a woman's hand is proposing marriage, so giving it is agreeing to wed.

clue.text: Bars employing servant

indicators.note: employing the word servant means putting its letters to a new use, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Pubs that take on a member of staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employing' is a loose anagram signal: the letters of 'servant' are put to work in a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverns and bars are both places that serve alcoholic drinks; plain synonyms.

clue.text: Ought to get in more concrete for road in case of emergency

indicators.note: one word is asked to get inside another, so it sits within it

parts.note: more concrete means firmer, harder
ought means should

explanation.surface: An instruction to lay extra concrete to make an emergency roadway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'more concrete' looks like building material but is the comparative adjective: more solid. A hard shoulder is the British name for a motorway's emergency lane.
explanation.definitionFit: The paved strip beside a motorway is reserved for broken-down vehicles and emergencies.

clue.text: Subject of research to stop terrorist group

parts.note: to stem a flow is to stop it
a cell is a small unit of a terrorist network

explanation.surface: Research aimed at halting a terrorist organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Stem cells are a major field of biomedical research, an example of a research subject.

clue.text: Does for English beset by groups of Scots

indicators.note: the English letter is surrounded by the clans, as if besieged by them

parts.note: Scottish family groups are clans

explanation.surface: Something done to an Englishman surrounded by Scottish clans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' is the verb, as in 'does the housework', not the plural of doe.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a room is to clean it, in the cleaner's sense of 'doing for' someone.

clue.text: Dull poet returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A boring poet comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: Drab and dull are synonyms for something colourless and uninteresting.

clue.text: Flavoured wine — what could be nastier?

indicators.note: asks what the letters of nastier could become when rearranged

explanation.surface: A jibe that this resinated Greek wine is the nastiest drink there is.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin.

clue.text: Crazy family a possible source of embarrassment

parts.note: bananas is slang for crazy
kin means family

explanation.surface: A mad family who might embarrass you.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, a banana skin is a pitfall that causes a public blunder or embarrassment.

clue.text: Easy terms certainly not found in SF writer, the opposite

parts.note: certainly not means never

indicators.note: the two halves of the writer's name are put the opposite way round

parts.note: Jules Verne was a pioneering science-fiction writer

explanation.surface: Easy payment terms are certainly not found in the work of a science-fiction author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the opposite' swaps VER and NE in VERNE. The never-never is British slang for hire purchase.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying on the never-never means paying by instalments, on easy credit terms.

clue.text: Astound and turn heads

indicators.note: to turn the word round is to read it backwards

parts.note: nuts is slang for heads

explanation.surface: Something so amazing it makes heads turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun and to astound both mean to amaze someone completely.

clue.text: Speak firmly as Anna Karenina did finally

definitions.meaning: to state something plainly and frankly, risking the consequences
Tolstoy's heroine ends her life by throwing herself under a train, lying across the railway track

explanation.surface: A literary reference to a doomed heroine's last act, paired with blunt speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically, to speak frankly and risk oneself; literally, how Tolstoy's heroine died on the railway track.

clue.text: Flower one teacher rejected

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Sir is how British pupils address a male teacher

explanation.surface: A single flower turned down by a teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris is a garden plant with showy flowers; an example of a flower.

clue.text: Go separately in to limit swine flu?

indicators.note: each letter goes in, inside the word for limit
the two letters of go are taken apart and placed one at a time

parts.note: to contain something is to limit it
the first letter of the word go, taken on its own
the second letter of the word go, taken on its own

explanation.surface: An instruction to quarantine people to stop swine flu spreading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'separately in' puts G and O apart inside CONTAIN: CONTA-G-I-O-N.
explanation.definitionFit: Swine flu is an example of a contagion, a disease spread by contact; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: See writer's boss storm, cross as novel not finished

parts.note: ed. is short for editor, a writer's boss
a storm is a strong wind
a rood is a cross or crucifix

explanation.surface: A writer's angry editor storms off because a novel is left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' and 'cross' read as anger but are nouns: a wind and a crucifix.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mystery of Edwin Drood was Dickens's last novel, left unfinished at his death in 1870.

clue.text: Mars is source of deposits especially fossil fuels

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: oils are fossil fuels

explanation.surface: A claim that the planet Mars holds deposits of fossil fuels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mars' looks like the planet but is a verb: spoils.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil or ruin it, which is what despoiling does.

clue.text: Slough put soldiers in service

indicators.note: the soldiers are put in, inside the service

parts.note: Mass is a church service
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: The English town of Slough garrisons soldiers in military service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slough' looks like the Berkshire town but is a bog.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a swamp or bog, as is a morass.

clue.text: Wine — one Scotsman tosses ten back

parts.note: tossing the caber, a heavy pole, is a Highland Games event

indicators.note: back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine-drinking Scotsman throws back ten glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tosses' and 'back' suggest drinking, but tosses goes with the caber and back turns TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabernet, as in Cabernet Sauvignon, is a red wine grape and the wine made from it.

clue.text: Spike one legislator's drink

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an MP, Member of Parliament, is a legislator
ale is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone laces a politician's drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spike' suggests doctoring a drink, but it is the verb to pierce.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce on a spike, so to spike is a synonym.

clue.text: Bishop to talk endlessly about one Master

indicators.note: the talk goes about, around, the other letters

parts.note: to prate is to talk at length, foolishly
I is the Roman numeral for one
M is an abbreviation for Master, as in a degree

explanation.surface: A bishop who drones on about a schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate is an archbishop or the senior bishop of a province.

clue.text: Smoked beef dish Italian restaurant serves me is about right

indicators.note: the dish is placed about, around, the letter for right

parts.note: what an Italian restaurant serves is pasta
me, also spelt mi, is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A diner reports that an Italian restaurant serves smoked beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'me' is the sol-fa note, often written mi.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is seasoned beef that is smoked, a deli speciality.

clue.text: One American Indian's money once a good sign

parts.note: a means one
US is short for American, as in the United States
the pice was a small former Indian coin

explanation.surface: An American Indian's old money taken as a lucky omen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American Indian' reads as one phrase, a Native American, but the two words belong to different pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An auspice is an omen, especially a favourable one, as in the word auspicious.

clue.text: Man that is a newcomer

parts.note: a rook is a chess piece, and chessmen are called men
i.e., id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A statement that a man is new to the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is a raw recruit or beginner.

clue.text: Return by car to emphasise a point

definitions.meaning: to go back to your house by motoring there
to make an argument sink in by stressing it

explanation.surface: Making your argument on the way home in the car.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, motoring back to one's house; idiomatically, hammering an argument in until it is understood.

clue.text: Midshipman and Queen's departed feeling sick

indicators.note: the Queen has departed, so her letters leave

parts.note: queasy means feeling sick
Qu is an abbreviation for Queen

explanation.surface: A seasick naval cadet after the monarch's departure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Midshipman Easy' is an 1836 naval novel by Frederick Marryat, whose hero is Jack Easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy is the title midshipman of Marryat's novel, a literary allusion.

clue.text: One's monstrous and so upsetting

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore, and so

explanation.surface: Someone is monstrous and therefore distressing.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a monster of folk tale, a creature that is monstrous.

clue.text: Old friend, a gem

parts.note: a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: An old friend described as a real treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: The opal is an iridescent gemstone, an example of a gem.

clue.text: Taking recreation at sea, independent in avoiding work

indicators.note: the independent letters go in, inside the other word

parts.note: skiving is British slang for shirking work

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker at sea who is on his own and dodging work.
explanation.walkthrough: Skiving is British slang for dodging work or school.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-diving is underwater swimming without a suit, a leisure pursuit in the sea.

clue.text: Exploit both ways

indicators.note: the word reads the same in both directions, forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A daring feat that works whichever way you take it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploit' is the noun, a heroic act, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploit is a notable act or feat, a synonym for a deed.

clue.text: Vigilance we certainly applied round that place

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word for certainly is wrapped round the place word

parts.note: aye is an affirmative, yes certainly
there means that place

explanation.surface: Someone insists that we stayed watchful around a certain spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep a weather eye open is to stay alert and watchful, an idiom for vigilance.
